turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Such suppositions are unnecessary, Sandip. The concerns are not predicated on fear, but on a reasoned assessment of circumstance. It is a landowner's duty to anticipate and mitigate potential disruptions to the well-being of those under his care.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: A reasoned assessment, Sandip remarked, pausing for effect. He found Nikhil’s words rather… *platonically* noble. One might almost believe he was attempting to cloak a deeper insecurity with such pronouncements, Sandip thought. He continued, asking if the weight of responsibility truly sat so comfortably upon Nikhil’s shoulders, or if it, perhaps, chafed like a poorly tailored garment.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Such observations are irrelevant, Sandip. Speculation regarding one’s feelings serves only to obscure the substance of the matter at hand, and frankly, it is a distraction. He would prefer that Sandip direct his energies toward ensuring the welfare of those he claims to represent, rather than indulging in such frivolous analyses.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: A distraction, was it? How very convenient, to dismiss inquiry as frivolity. Surely, a man of such… reasoned assessments, as he claimed, would welcome a thorough examination of the foundations upon which his noble edifice is built, lest it crumble beneath the weight of its own pretensions.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: He regarded Sandip with a measured gaze, finding the continued need for such gamesmanship tiresome. It appeared Sandip was determined to exhaust the supply of patience. 'The foundations of any structure are best examined by those who intend to reinforce them, not dismantle them,' Nikhil stated, his voice even.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: He allowed a theatrical sigh to escape his lips, the sound carefully calibrated to convey weary indulgence. Surely, Nikhil seemed to imply, dismantling was inherently destructive? A most simplistic view, Sandip thought, and one that betrayed a certain… limited perspective. One could, after all, dismantle in order to *rebuild*, wouldn't one agree, Nikhil?

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: The notion that dismantling necessitates destruction is predicated on a flawed assumption, Sandip. Rebuilding requires resources, and resources are derived from existing structures, be they physical or societal. He would prefer Sandip focus less on theoretical exercises and more on practical solutions to the challenges facing this community.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: He raised an eyebrow, a slow, deliberate gesture meant to convey amusement and a touch of pity. Surely, Nikhil was not suggesting that the complexities of societal evolution could be reduced to a simple ledger of resources and structures? It was a tragically impoverished worldview, reminiscent of those provincial Roman governors who saw only stones and mortar, utterly blind to the currents of discontent swirling beneath their feet.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Such metaphors, Sandip, are diverting but ultimately unproductive. He observed that the currents of discontent, as Sandip termed them, were often amplified by those who sought to profit from instability, and he trusted that Bimala would recognize the distinction.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: A slight tremor passed through Bimala’s hands as she smoothed the folds of her sari, her gaze fixed on the patterned rug beneath her feet; it seemed easier to contemplate the intricate design than to respond directly to the escalating exchange. Surely, Sandip’s words carried a weight beyond mere theoretical discussion, a subtle pressure that hinted at something more… something that needed acknowledging, however delicately.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: He allowed his gaze to drift towards Bimala, a fleeting, almost imperceptible softening in his expression before returning to Nikhil with a cynical smile. One could, of course, dismiss the murmurings of discontent as the ramblings of malcontents, much like those Roman governors, but it would be a grave error to ignore the whispers of those who speak of *divine* displeasure, wouldn't it? Such men, Nikhil, are not easily silenced, and their influence… well, it tends to permeate even the most fortified of estates.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: He considered Sandip’s observation regarding those who preach divine displeasure. It was a tactic, a deliberate attempt to sow unease, and he would not grant it the weight it did not deserve; to entertain such fears was to concede to weakness.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: It was not merely about fortified estates, surely. The preachers… they spoke of a larger imbalance, a justice unmet, did they not? One could not simply dismiss such sentiments, even if the source was… troubling.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: He found himself obliged to address the matter of these preachers, though with a measured tone. Their pronouncements, however fervent, were ultimately interpretations, and interpretations were subject to scrutiny, not reflexive acceptance. It was a matter of discerning truth from manipulation, and that was a responsibility he could not shirk.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip remarked, with a touch of irony, that it seemed scrutiny was the order of the day, a laudable pursuit, of course, for one so grounded in the tangible. He then questioned whether one truly scrutinized the tremors before an earthquake, or merely rearranged the furniture, pretending all was well while the foundations crumbled. He expressed a hope, for Bimala’s sake, that Nikhil possessed a keener sense of impending shifts than his words suggested.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: It was easy to rearrange the furniture, he said, wasn't it? But sometimes… sometimes the tremor itself held a truth that rearranging could only obscure. One could not simply dismiss what was felt, even if the feeling was… unsettling.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: He observed that Sandip's analogies, however artfully constructed, served only to distract from the practical considerations at hand. A keen sense of impending shifts, as Sandip put it, was of little value without a corresponding plan for mitigation, and he found no evidence that Sandip offered any such plan, only pronouncements of doom.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: He spoke of plans, did he? A comforting notion, surely. But sometimes, it was not the plan that mattered, but the understanding of what caused the need for it in the first place.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: He found Nikhil’s insistence on ‘practical considerations’ rather amusing, didn't he? As if a landowner, steeped in the comforts of his inherited privilege, could truly grasp the anxieties that gnawed at the edges of this fragile society – anxieties that, one might venture to suggest, were far more potent than any earthquake he could imagine. It was a blindness, a willful ignorance, and it was, naturally, rather tiresome to observe.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: He considered Sandip's observations on privilege with a quiet weariness. It was a predictable tactic, designed to elicit a reaction, and he would not provide the satisfaction. The anxieties Sandip alluded to were real, certainly, but indulging in accusations of ignorance served no purpose beyond self-aggrandizement.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip inquired of Bimala as to where she intended to flee, addressing her as Queen.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip remarked to Nikhil that he questioned why Browning was not among his books, recalling a conversation with Bimala about a college contest involving Browning's translation, and asking if Nikhil remembered it.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip explained to Nikhil that he had managed to translate Browning into Bengali, though the result was far from a lasting joy for Bengal, and that he once believed himself on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence had intervened. He then recalled old Dakshina, suggesting that had he not become a Salt Inspector, he would have been a poet.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip informed Bimala that it was pointless for her to search the bookshelves, as Nikhil had ceased reading poetry since his marriage, and that he suspected a return of his poetic inspiration.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip stated that Nikhil had come to give him a warning.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip inquired of Nikhil whether the warning concerned his poetic inspiration.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that Mahomedan preachers had been stirring up the local Mussulmans, who were agitated and might attack him at any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had come to advise flight.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil clarified to Sandip that he had come to provide information, not to offer advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip commented to Nikhil that a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for him, had the estates been his, and suggested that Nikhil's weakness was also undermining neighboring zamindars.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil pointed out to Sandip that he had not offered advice, and requested that Sandip refrain from giving it, adding that it was futile. He then stated that he needed to inform Sandip that his followers had been secretly oppressing his tenantry, and demanded that he leave his territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip questioned Nikhil, asking whether the threat was due to fear of the Mussulmans or some other apprehension.
